summary:
JAM is a cooperative survival game where kids lead a crew on Mars. One to four players share a base and four connected resources: water, oxygen, energy and food. They expand the base to reach 10 investigation sites before any resource runs out. Along the way they face random Martian hazards: solar storms, water leaks, oxygen loss and rotten food. Each one has to be spotted and fixed using energy.

Every map is built from real Martian terrain. Our server samples NASA HiRISE elevation data from four real places on Mars, including Jezero Crater, where the Perseverance rover landed. Kids explore actual Martian landscapes, not invented ones.

JAM answers the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning real mission limits into gameplay. Resources drain faster than they refill, and building costs water, oxygen and energy, so every choice is a trade-off. Players have to communicate, plan ahead and stay calm when an alarm goes off. These are the same skills real astronauts train for. JAM makes space science hands-on and teaches teamwork and decision-making under pressure.
details:
What it does and how it works
JAM is a cooperative Mars survival game played in a web browser by 1–4 players. The team starts in a small 3×3 base on a 50×50-cell map that represents a real 500 m × 500 m patch of Mars.

  • Resources: the base’s stash slowly generates water, oxygen, energy and food. The team’s shared supply always drains faster, so players must keep moving to the stash to collect.
  • Goal: expand the base one tile at a time until it covers all 10 investigation sites. Each tile costs water, oxygen and energy. If any resource reaches zero, the mission fails.
  • Hazards: every 30 seconds the game may trigger an event. A solar storm (mild or strong) cuts production. A water leak or oxygen loss makes that resource drain 50% faster. Rotten food wipes out part of the food supply instantly. Players spend energy to repair storms and leaks, guided by alarms, alert banners and a mission minimap.
  • Behind the scenes: a Go server runs the official game state and sends it to every player in real time over WebSockets, so all teammates see the same thing at the same moment.

Benefits

  • Learning by doing: kids experience how life-support resources depend on each other instead of memorizing facts.
  • Real science: every map is real Martian terrain from NASA HiRISE elevation data of Jezero Crater, Russell Crater’s dunes, the Gigas Sulci channels and Candor Chasma.
  • Teamwork and communication: resources are shared, so players have to coordinate who collects, who builds and who repairs.
  • Decision-making under pressure: resources always drain and hazards strike without warning, so kids practice staying calm, setting priorities and accepting trade-offs.
  • Easy access: it runs in a web browser with nothing to install, so it works at home or in a classroom.

Intended impact
We want kids to see themselves as future explorers and understand what real astronauts face: limited resources, a hostile environment and the need to work as a team. JAM gives teachers and parents a fun starting point for STEM topics like atmosphere, radiation, planetary geography and systems thinking. It also gives kids a safe place to fail, learn and try again.

Tools, coding languages, hardware and software

  • Client (front end): TypeScript, React and Three.js for 3D graphics, built with Vite and Bun.
  • Server (back end): Go, with a documented WebSocket protocol and a reference test bot.
  • Data processing: Python and GDAL to turn NASA/JPL/University of Arizona HiRISE elevation models into game maps at 10 m resolution.
  • Deployment and testing: Docker, Docker Compose and Nginx, with automated tests on both client and server, all managed on GitHub.
  • Hardware: none required beyond a standard computer with a modern web browser.

How it’s creative
JAM turns scientific data into gameplay instead of a quiz. Players aren’t told that Mars is hard; they feel it, because the game is designed so resources always run out. Each map number (a “seed”) always loads the same real patch of Mars, so every match can happen on a different authentic landscape. Hazards appear at random, so no two missions play out the same. Cooperative play replaces competition: the only enemy is Mars itself.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific accuracy: we used only real measured elevations and invented no terrain. We documented where the data came from and credited NASA/JPL/University of Arizona.
  • Game balance: we tuned drain rates, building costs, repair costs and hazard chances so the game is tense but winnable.
  • Age-appropriateness: a friendly cartoon style and clear icons and alerts, with no violence or combat.
  • Accessibility: browser-based, works for solo or team play, needs no special hardware.
  • Fairness and reliability: the server is the single source of truth, so all players stay in sync, and automated tests make sure the game behaves as expected.
  • Room to grow: the architecture is ready for future features like matchmaking, leaderboards and more Mars regions.
